summary: Only the southern rim of Kazakhstan (Isfijab/Sayram, Taraz, Otrar, Jand, Semirechye) came under caliph-recognising dynasties: the Samanids, the Karakhanids after c.1001 and the Khwarazmshahs. No caliphal governor ever ruled the northern, central or western steppe, whose first Muslim rulers were the Islamised Golden Horde (from 1313), the Nogai Horde and the Kazakh khans. The Kimek-Kipchak and Oghuz confederations were not Muslim states, and the Qara Khitai (1130s-1211) were non-Muslim overlords. Russia absorbed the steppe between the 1730s and 1860s.

units.notes: Isfijab was taken from the Turks by the Samanid Nuh b. Asad in 840 but kept its own Turkic dynasty, which showed loyalty by military service, gifts and the Samanid name on coins: a vassal of a caliph-recognising dynasty. Karakhanid rule from 980 became caliph-recognising from c.1001; Otrar had a Khwarazmshah governor in 1218. Russian conquest of Chimkent 1864.

units.label: Mangyshlak (Manqishlaq)

caliphate.who: Khwarazmshah Atsiz (Seljuk vassal, Abbasid-recognising dynasty) occupied the peninsula
caliphate.dates: 1127 or 1138 to 1221 (dates conflict between sources; depth of administration unknown)

units.notes: Mangyshlak was nomad country (Oghuz/Turkmen, later Kazakh), on the border between Khwarazm and the Khazars. Its one link to a caliph-recognising state is the Khwarazmshah occupation from Atsiz's time to the Mongols (1221); it was never under direct caliphal governors. Kalmyks (Buddhist) took or raided it from 1620/1639; Russia built forts in 1834 and 1846 and Khiva renounced its claim in 1873.
units.uncertain: Sources disagree on Atsiz's date (1127 in the Mangystau Region article vs 1138 in the Atsiz article) and none I opened describes how long or how deeply the Khwarazmshahs governed it; if their hold was brief this should drop to 'temporary' and the unit would be 'islamic_state_ruled' (Golden Horde/Nogai). Bosworth's EI2 article 'Mangishlak' was not accessible.

summary: Almost all of Uzbekistan was conquered by the Umayyads under Qutayba b. Muslim (705-715) and then ruled directly by Umayyad and Abbasid governors, though the Turgesh rolled much of it back between 720 and 738. Outlying principalities (Khwarazm, Chaghaniyan, Ushrusana, Shash, Ferghana) were first tributaries and came under Abbasid and Samanid rule between 751 and 893. After the Mongols, Muslim states that did not recognise a caliph ruled: the Chagatayids, Timurids, Shaybanids and the khanates of Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand. Russia conquered it between 1865 and 1876.

summary: Southern Turkmenistan (Merv, Nasa, Abivard, Sarakhs) was part of Khurasan and fell to the Rashidun caliphate in 651, staying under caliphal and caliph-recognising rule until the Mongols. Khwarazm (Dashoguz) and Dihistan (Balkan) were first tributary or briefly conquered and later ruled by caliph-recognising dynasties. After 1220, Muslim states that did not recognise a caliph followed: the Golden Horde, Timurids, Khiva, Bukhara and Iran. The Turkmen tribes were independent until the Russian conquest of 1881-1885.

units.notes: Merv was taken without a fight in 651, when Yazdegerd III died nearby, and became the capital of Umayyad Khurasan and the launching point of the Abbasid revolution. The Mongols destroyed it in 1221; Russia occupied the oasis in 1884.

summary: No Umayyad or Abbasid governor ever ruled Kyrgyz territory except the Ferghana valley, which the Samanids governed for the caliph from 819. The Chu valley, Talas and Issyk-Kul came under Muslim rule through the Karakhanids, whose capital was Balasagun and who recognised the Abbasids from about 1001, until the non-Muslim Qara Khitai took over in 1134. Later Muslim states were Moghulistan (Muslim khans from 1354) and Kokand (early 19th c.), separated by long Kyrgyz tribal and Dzungar periods. Russia took the north in the 1850s-60s and Kokand in 1876.

units.notes: The valley floor around Osh, Uzgend and Jalal-Abad was part of medieval Farghana, which Arab geographers (al-Muqaddasi, Ibn Hawqal) described; the surrounding mountains were held by pastoral tribes. Russia annexed it with Kokand in 1876.
units.uncertain: Whether Samanid control reached the eastern valley (Osh, Uzgend) or only the western and central valley was not confirmed; the Karakhanid status is solid. The classical geographers are cited only as reported on the Ozgon Wikipedia page, not seen directly.

summary: Northern Tajikistan (Panjikant, Ushrusana, Khujand) and Khuttal in the south were conquered and ruled under the Umayyads and Abbasids, Ushrusana only from 822 and Khuttal fully from 750-751, and then by the Samanids and Ghaznavids. The Hisar/Dushanbe area was probably Samanid, but the evidence is thin. Karategin and the Pamirs (Gorno-Badakhshan) kept their own princes or mirs and came under larger Muslim states (Bukhara, Afghanistan) only in the 1870s-1890s. Bukhara ruled most of the country under Russian protection until 1920-21.

units.notes: Wikipedia says the Samanids controlled the Dushanbe region after the Arab conquest. The mountain district of Karategin (Rasht) stayed under native princes until Bukhara annexed it (1868/1877). units.uncertain: The only evidence for early caliphal-era rule here is one sentence in the Wikipedia Dushanbe article (the same article misplaces Hulbuk, which is in Khatlon, 'near Dushanbe'). Karategin's early-Islamic status (said to have been independent 'for many centuries'; one passage claims Bukharan conquest in 1636) is unresolved.

units.notes: No caliphal or caliph-recognising state is documented in the Pamir valleys. The region was ruled by small Muslim mirdoms (Darvaz, Shughnan-Rushan, Wakhan) and from the 1870s-1890s by Afghanistan and Bukhara, with Russia completing control in 1895-96. Ismaili Islam spread here mainly through missionary activity, not conquest.
units.uncertain: Whether any of the Pamir valleys paid tribute to the Abbasids or Samanids (as part of greater Badakhshan) was not checked; Iranica's Badakhshan/Shughnan articles were not reached. The Shughnan Wikipedia summary has inconsistent 1874/1883/1893 dates. The role of Nasir-i Khusraw in Ismaili conversion is widely reported but not checked here.
